extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, and serious readers studying the craft of the modern novel
extracted.subtask_description: A practical-critical guide to how novels are made and how they should be read and judged, focusing on form, selection, point of view, scene vs picture, and technical narrative methods. Aimed at helping writers choose disciplined methods and critics/readers to reconstruct a book's shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form / Shape of the Book
rubrics_metrics.description: A book has a form — a shape or design — which can be ascribable as good or bad; the critic's task is to detect and judge that form even though the novel reaches the reader as a flowing procession of impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novel, when re-created by a critical reader, stands as a single, coherent, welded mass. Consider whether the book's form expresses its subject fully and compactly. Anti-patterns: treating a novel merely as a succession of vivid scenes or characters without assessing the overall outline; calling 'form' optional because life is messy. Examples in text: Tolstoy's War and Peace (huge panorama—form questioned) and Flaubert/Bovary (scenes affirm structural lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and Arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's essential craft is in selecting portions of life (what to keep, what to discard) and arranging them into an artful order; selection and arrangement determine the book's intelligible form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author's selection springs from the heart of the subject and whether arrangement follows a true development of that subject. Look for signs of divergence from the subject or arbitrary detours. Anti-patterns: gratuitous episodes that don't serve subject or design; unmotivated digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / Coherence of Design
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel should cohere: chapter-to-chapter and scene-to-scene relations should cumulatively express the subject; imperfections in form usually mean the subject is imperfectly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the finished shape expresses one central idea or subject and whether any parts contradict or disregard that subject. When form is faulty, probe whether the fault arises from treatment or from a weak subject. Example: the critic's question 'What is the story?' posed for War and Peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the Dramatic Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident or scene is the most important instrument: it gives the sharpest, final effect (the 'final stroke') and should be used to clinch matters already prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scene sparingly and strategically: place dramatized scenes where they confirm or crown previously built effects; avoid overusing dialogue/drama when it accomplishes nothing. Anti-patterns: wasting the scene on material that could be conveyed more economically by narrative; scenes that are unprepared and therefore slow or diffuse. Example: Bovary's well-wrought dramatised scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and Appropriateness of Modes (Scene vs Narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different narrative modes (dramatic scene, pictorial/general survey, panoramic description, generalized narrative) have different costs and strengths and must be used where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author uses each mode for its natural purpose: scenes for clinching action, picture for long reaches and accumulated impressions, narrative summary for economical covering of time/space. Penalize misuses: dramatizing what should be summarized wastes time and weakens climax; over-reliance on picture makes narrative thin unless compensated by dramatizing the character of the mind that perceives it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Picture / Pictorial Narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial or panoramic treatments travel over time and space and accumulate impressions; they perform functions different from the scene and are valuable when a long reach or survey is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether pictorial passages are used to pile up necessary impressions and whether they are balanced with drama so climax and clarity are achieved. Anti-patterns: thin, flat pictorial reports that merely mirror external facts without dramatizing the perceiving mind; failing to convert the weakness of pictorial mode into strength by emphasizing the narrator's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of Time and Space
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene cannot foreshorten time or space — it displays the whole time and space it occupies; narrative and picture can compress or extend time and space economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author uses scene and narration in ways that respect their temporal/spatial properties. Look for economical summary where breadth is needed and for dramatized scenes where immediacy and visibility are required. Anti-patterns: scenes that attempt to cover long durations (inefficient), or summaries that obscure crucial immediate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View / Narratorial Limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice and discipline of point of view (whose consciousness or voice mediates the story) is a central technical decision; different choices (omniscient authorial voice, restricted consciousness, minstrel/authorial licence) produce different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the POV chosen suits the subject and whether the narrator's freedoms are coherently maintained. Minstrel/authorial licence (an unconstrained storyteller) can be effective only for certain minds; otherwise a disciplined limitation usually makes for better concentration and effect. Anti-patterns: casual shifts of authorial stance that undermine unity; 'minstrel's licence' used as an easy way out that narrows the story's potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological / Consciousness-centred Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling a story through a constituted mind (centred consciousness) converts mere pictorial report into a dramatized presentation because the mind (the mirror) becomes visible and active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the solidity and dramatic value of stories centred in a character's consciousness: has the author used the mind as an instrument to dramatize and add depth to pictorial material? Anti-patterns: failing to make the perceiving mind vivid when relying on pictorial narrative, resulting in flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization (Command of Life)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist's 'command of life' — the ability to render characters vivid, convincing, and lasting in memory — is a primary measure of success; characters should persist as 'positive facts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether characters are made intelligible and vivid enough to survive the reader's imperfect memory; look for depth, consistency, and individuality. Examples: Richardson's Clarissa, Tolstoy's Anna, Flaubert's Emma as enduring presences. Anti-patterns: characters that are merely types or sketches without inner reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Subject and the Author's Eye
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist's selection of subject — discovering the fruitful idea in life that will sustain a book — is the cardinal gift; after the subject is found, craft issues begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the appropriateness and fertility of the subject for novelistic treatment and whether the author's subsequent choices (point of view, modes, selection) respect the subject's demands. If the subject is poor, even technical skill cannot always rescue the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment Suited to Stage of Development
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must have a working theory of which instrument (scene, picture, panorama, narrative) is appropriate at each stage of the story's development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the treatments used at particular points (opening, development, climax, denouement) are appropriate to those narrative tasks. Look for scenes used to crown issues that have been prepared and for picture or summary used to provide background or breadth. Anti-patterns: consistent reliance on a single mode that ill-fits different stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Wastage of Dramatic Strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the scene is 'expensive' in time/space, it must not be called upon to do work it cannot do; scenes should be prepared and reserved for their highest uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novel conserves dramatic opportunities and places scenes where they have maximal effect. Anti-patterns: frequent unprepared dramatizations, scene-by-scene presentation of trivial matters that dissipate the novel's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Knowledge of Narrative Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic (and novelist) must know the different narrative forms and be able to recognize and use them consciously; these include dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized, panoramic, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author demonstrates command of these narrative devices and whether the critic/reader recognizes them when reconstructing the book. This is a prerequisite for constructive criticism of 'how the book was made.' Anti-patterns: sloppy or unreflected mixture of modes that obscures the book's technical aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's Active Reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a novel properly the reader must read 'creatively' — re-create the book in the mind as a single form rather than simply enjoying detached scenes and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should attempt to reassemble the book's intended form by keeping the world at a distance and reconstructing the author's selection and arrangement. This is also presented as the critic's craft: to make a book out of the impressions given and then judge its making. Anti-patterns: passive reading that yields only fleeting impressions and cannot support precise critical statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Shyness/Delicacy in Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not be inhibited by a romantic scruple that the novel is 'a piece of life' and therefore should escape analysis; a novel is an art object and may be dissected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage frank technical analysis: dissect design, proportion, and devices without fearing to 'spoil the pleasure of illusion.' Anti-patterns: weak criticism that excuses faults because the novel 'captures life.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of Methodological Weakness into Strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods with inherent disabilities (e.g., pictorial report's thinness) can be turned into strengths by emphasizing what they can uniquely show (e.g., the perceiving mind as a visible object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author has acknowledged a mode's weakness and used it self-consciously to obtain a new effect (e.g., making the narrator's mind a dramatized object). Anti-patterns: unquestioned adoption of a weak mode leading to flatness; failure to dramatize the 'mirror' (mind) when using pictorial narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and Proportion in Large Works
rubrics_metrics.description: In very large, panoramic novels (wide scope, many characters, long spans) the problem of effective composition and proportion becomes acute and must be judged: is the work 'neatly composed' or merely a prodigality of invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large works, examine whether parts are lucid and shapely even if the whole resists neat composition; consider if the apparent shapelessness hides an underlying organizing idea, or if the work lacks a definable subject. Example: War and Peace—parts are lucid though the whole prompts the question 'What is the story?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious Use of Authorial Freedom (Minstrel Licence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unconstrained storyteller's voice (the minstrel) imposes no limitation and tells what he pleases; this licence is appropriate only to certain writers and certain stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the authorial freedom used serves the story or is a lazy choice. If the minstrel's licence is taken without the necessary gifts, the story is narrowed and diminished. Anti-patterns: choosing ease over disciplined method; using omniscience as a convenience rather than as a deliberate artistic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of Subject-to-Treatment Relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a clear relation between the subject discovered and the subsequent handling — the treatment should grow naturally from the subject's demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the course the author pursues (ordering, modes, emphasis) follows from the subject's logic; if not, name and evaluate alternatives. Anti-patterns: treatment that seems to disregard the subject or takes gratuitous turns unrelated to the central idea.
